attributes.date: RR 189 — fourteen years before the present
attributes.distance_to_the_centre: eight hundred miles is Bell Harrow to Tallow Reach, rim to rim. The centre is half of that from either side — roughly 385 miles: twenty days at a laden pace, about fifteen for a rider in a forced run. Anyone who argues that the Wardenry cannot reach the survey site in time is using the width of the plain for the reach of it, and doubling his own answer.
attributes.eleven_days: the speed is the point — the Wardenry had a Warden of the Third Rank standing on the spoil-heap inside eleven days, forty miles out. Most of that was Bell Harrow making up its mind; the ride was under two days in either direction. The riding is not what buys anyone time, and it never was.
attributes.outcome: ground sealed under the Fourth Article, shaft capped with plain-salt and mortar, compensation paid at the last assessed price of salt
attributes.status: the seal is in its fourteenth year and still in force. The assay was done on the day of the declaration; the hazard survey has never been begun. Ferrant died in RR 197.
attributes.the_assay: a Wardenry glass, floated on the spoil-heap the morning the Warden arrived, before the two witnesses the Article requires — both of them Wardenry men. The reference brine in it had been drawn and sealed at Bell Harrow by the Wardenry, so the body with the interest calibrated the instrument, read it, and wrote down the reading. The College of Levels never certified that glass and has never been shown it. Within the week the shaft was capped with plain-salt and mortar, and there has been nothing to sample since. One morning's work by one interested party is the whole of what is known about the water under Ferrant's ground.
attributes.the_clock_it_changes: fifteen days out and fifteen back roughly halves the response everyone assumes. News leaving the centre puts a Warden of the Third Rank in the survey camp inside a month, and the Fourth Article's forty days to enter a seal on the Bell Harrow roll is comfortable rather than impossible — a rider who speaks the declaration at the centre has twenty-five days of slack to get it onto the roll. So chapter 5 does not turn on whether they can arrive. They can. It turns on the season clock, and only a licence-holder standing on the sealed ground can start it.
attributes.the_survey_that_never_began: the seal was granted 'until the hazard is surveyed and lifted', and in fourteen years the Wardenry has not appointed a surveyor. No depth stands on any roll, no volume, no second reading, no finding anyone can dispute — there is nothing to argue with, which is the point. Ferrant asked in RR 190 and again in RR 193 and was told the surveyor was not yet appointed. He was still asking when he died.
attributes.two_different_threats: the assay and the missing survey are not one failure and they do not produce the same chapter. 'They seal it and never look again' means the centre goes quiet for fourteen years and Ysoly's tile is the only thing on the plain that can make anyone look. 'They look, call it brackish, and never let you check' means a man stands in the survey camp, says one word, and ends the argument — and the whole question becomes who is permitted to hold the glass. Ferrant got both. The difference at the centre is that this time a College-sealed glass is already on the ground, in the hands of a Warden-surveyor, and the Wardenry has no way to be the only reader in the room.
attributes.what_ferrant_did_not_have: a crossing licence for the ground he was standing on, and therefore no season clock to force. He could only take the money. This is the single difference between Ferrant and Ysoly Tamm.
attributes.what_was_found: water at ninety feet, forty miles onto the plain. Called brackish on the day of the declaration, on the Wardenry's own assay, and never tested by anybody else since.
attributes.who: Ferrant, a rim merchant. The declaring Warden's name is on the roll at Bell Harrow and can be looked up by anyone who asks.
attributes.why_it_matters: it is the working precedent — the exact shape of what the Wardenry will do at the centre, already done once, cleanly, and never challenged. Everyone who is about to argue about the Fourth Article is really arguing about Ferrant.

name: The Ferrant Sinking
summary: A rim merchant named Ferrant sank a shaft forty miles onto the plain, hit water at ninety feet, and had a Warden of the Third Rank standing on his spoil-heap inside eleven days. The water was assayed on the heap that morning and called brackish; the ground was declared a hazard, the shaft capped with plain-salt and mortar, and Ferrant paid the worth of forty miles of crust at the assessed salt price — enough to keep him quiet, not enough to make him rich. Fourteen years on the seal has never been lifted, the hazard survey it was granted for has never been begun, and nobody outside the Wardenry has ever been permitted to draw a second sample.
